data.title: Actinic keratosis — viva
data.summary: Premalignant & malignant tumours · 10 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Actinic keratosis** (Premalignant & malignant tumours)_

**Q1. Define actinic keratosis (AK).**
- UV-induced intra-epidermal proliferation of atypical keratinocytes on chronically sun-damaged skin (solar keratosis) — regarded as SCC in situ (early) / premalignant; marker of field cancerisation
- Fair-skinned elderly, outdoor workers, immunosuppressed (transplant recipients); uncommon in Indian skin types except albinos and farmers

**Q2. Clinical features and variants.**
- Rough, sandpaper-like, scaly red/skin-coloured macules or papules (better felt than seen) on face, scalp (bald), ears, dorsa of hands, forearms; background photodamage
- Variants: hypertrophic, atrophic, pigmented, lichenoid, bowenoid, cutaneous horn, actinic cheilitis (lower lip — scaling, blurred vermilion border)

**Q3. Risk of progression to SCC.**
- Individual AK: ~0.1–0.6% per year (up to 10% over 10 years); ~60% of SCCs arise from AKs; some regress spontaneously
- Warning signs: induration, inflammation, diameter >1 cm, rapid growth, bleeding, ulceration, pain (IFRBU)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Atypical keratinocytes in the basal layer extending upward, alternating ortho- and parakeratosis ('flag sign' — parakeratosis over atypical epidermis, orthokeratosis over spared adnexal ostia), solar elastosis, budding of basal layer; Olsen grading (AK I–III)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Seborrhoeic keratosis (stuck-on), SCC in situ/Bowen's, superficial BCC, DLE, porokeratosis (DSAP), lichen planus-like keratosis, solar lentigo (pigmented AK), arsenical keratoses (palms/soles), wart

**Q6. Management.**
- Lesion-directed: cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen — most common), curettage and cautery, excision/biopsy for suspicious lesions, CO2 laser
- Field-directed: 5-fluorouracil 0.5–5% cream, imiquimod 3.75–5%, diclofenac 3% gel, tirbanibulin 1% (5-day course — microtubule/Src inhibitor), photodynamic therapy (ALA/MAL + red/blue light or daylight PDT), chemical peels, ablative laser resurfacing
- Prevention: daily sunscreen (reduces new AKs), nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily (reduces new AK/NMSC in high-risk), acitretin chemoprevention in transplant recipients; regular skin checks

**Q7. What is field cancerisation and why treat the field?**
- Chronic UV damage produces clinically invisible genetic alterations (p53 mutant clones) over the whole sun-exposed area; treating only visible AKs misses subclinical lesions — field therapies treat the whole area

**Q8. Field therapies and their details.**
- 5-fluorouracil 5% cream twice daily for 2–4 weeks (or 0.5% with salicylic acid); imiquimod 5% 2–3 times/week for 4–16 weeks or 3.75% daily cycles; diclofenac 3% gel 90 days (mild); ingenol mebutate (withdrawn — skin cancer signal); tirbanibulin 1% ointment once daily for 5 days (tubulin/Src inhibitor — newer); PDT with ALA/MAL (conventional or daylight); chemical peels, ablative laser resurfacing
- Calcipotriol + 5-FU combination (short, immune-enhancing); oral nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily reduces new AKs and NMSC in high-risk patients (ONTRANS/ONTRAC)

**Q9. Grading of AK (Olsen) and clinical clues to SCC.**
- Olsen grade I (more palpable than visible), II (moderately thick, easily seen), III (very thick, hyperkeratotic)
- Red flags for invasive SCC (IDRBEU): Induration/inflammation, Diameter >1 cm, Rapid enlargement, Bleeding, Erythema, Ulceration — biopsy

**Q10. Who are high-risk patients?**
- Organ-transplant recipients (on immunosuppressants — 65–250× SCC risk), CLL, HIV, prior skin cancers, albinism, XP, chronic voriconazole use, long-term PUVA, heavy sun exposure in fair skin — need regular skin surveillance and aggressive field treatment

## Quick spotter facts
- Rough sandpaper scaly papules on bald scalp of an elderly farmer — AK
- Flag sign on histology
- Field therapy: 5-FU, imiquimod, PDT, tirbanibulin

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Premalignant epidermal lesions). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
